en: The Aṅgulimāla Sūtra, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi Nation during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with [the assembly].
He was accompanied by a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.

In the city of Śrāvastī, there was a certain brahmin who had extensively mastered the three Vedas without any doubt or obstruction; he fully expounded the five classics and answered immediately whatever was asked of him. His brilliance shone throughout the lecture halls, and all looked up to him with reverence. The elders of the state consulted him, and among the scholars, he was their preeminent master. His disciples were numerous, numbering five hundred.

The foremost disciple was named Aṅgulimāla (translated into Chinese as Zhǐmàn, "Finger-Garland"). His physical frame was robust and fierce, and his strength surpassed that of a mighty warrior; with his hands he could catch birds in flight, beasts running wild, or horses charging ahead. He was intelligent, talented, and eloquent, with a gentle and refined disposition. He was composed, quick-witted, and free from all doubt or obstruction; his physical appearance was unsurpassed, and he was held in high esteem by his teacher.
The mistress of the house, filled with reverence, waited for her husband to go out on his rounds;

she went to find Aṅgulimāla and said to him, "Observing your countenance, you possess a dignified and noble air. Judging by your age, I see we are not much different. Might we share our joys together and enjoy each other's company?"
Upon hearing this, Aṅgulimāla was struck with panic and terror; his hair stood on end as he knelt and replied, "Madam, you have been my mother and my teacher, and thus you are like a father to me.
I dare not accept such an instruction, for my heart finds it distasteful and it is utterly contrary to the Dharma."
The teacher’s wife spoke again:
“To give food to the hungry and water to the thirsty—what in this is contrary to the Dharma?
To bestow warm clothing upon those who are cold and provide coolness to those who are hot—what in this is contrary to the Dharma?”
"To clothe those who are naked and to rescue those in peril— what in this is contrary to the Dharma?
Aṅgulimāla replied, "To hasten to the aid of those in urgent distress and to provide relief to the destitute— truly, there is nothing here that is contrary to the Dharma."

"The lady is my mother, and she is one whom the Teacher holds in high esteem; yet you have followed your lust, become attached to her form, and out of arrogance committed what was improper—like a snake or a lizard that has swallowed poison.

Upon hearing this in the Teacher’s chamber, she immediately felt shame and resentment. Returning home, she tore her garments to pieces, smeared her face with saffron, and lay prostrate in feigned grief.
Then, when her husband returned from his journey, he asked:
"For what reason? What evil has occurred?
Who has troubled or provoked you?"
The wife slandered him, saying:

"The disciple whom you have always praised for his intelligence, who is gentle, kind, upright, and pure in conduct without flaw—when you were away this morning, he came and seized me by force. He wished to indulge in perverse insolence, and though I did not comply, I was instead insulted, assaulted, and crushed until I was utterly exhausted; it is for this reason that I am humiliated and cannot rise."

Upon hearing this, the Master was despondent and his mind filled with intense anger; he wished to inflict corporal punishment and suppress the wickedness through forceful treatment, yet he feared that the man’s formidable dominance was beyond his power to subdue. Retreating, he desired to remain silent and contemplate deeply how such unrighteousness had defiled the inner chambers and thrown the hierarchy into disorder. He pondered back and forth, wondering what he should do.
Thereupon, he sighed with deep distress and said:
"I must slightly alter the common and inverted teachings to instruct them; I shall teach them to kill until the limit of one hundred, each piercing a finger to form a garland upon their foreheads."
The crime of killing is the greatest of all sins!

If one does not inflict severe and cruel punishment, the offender will surely be executed; they will suffer immediate peril and death, and after death fall into hell, from which there is no release—even if one were to let them go, the consequences would only increase further.
Thereupon, the Master summoned Aṅgulimāla and addressed him, saying:

"Your intelligence is sharp and your learning is thorough; you have ascended to the hall and entered the inner chamber, and your cultivation is as profound as it is without beginning. It is only this one art that you have not yet put into practice."
Aṅgulimāla stepped forward and said,
"I wish to hear what has been told.
The Teacher said:

"One who desires rapid success should take up a sharp sword and, at dawn, personally kill one hundred people at a crossroads, taking a finger from each person as an ornament for their adornment, until midday when the full number of one hundred fingers is obtained."
"If you establish diligent devotion and compliance, then your Way and virtue will be complete.
He then handed over the sword. Aṅgulimāla accepted the sword;
hearing this instruction, he was struck with alarm and fear, his heart filled with sorrow and distress.

"If I were to violate the teachings, I would not be a filial disciple; if I follow them, I fear falling into error. He bowed with his sword and withdrew, weeping as he said: "To purely cultivate the Brahma-conduct is the Dharma of a Brahmin;

to filially support one's parents is the Dharma of a Brahmin; to cultivate all manner of good deeds is the Dharma of a Brahmin; to abandon the heterodox and correctly take refuge is the Dharma of a Brahmin; to be gentle, kind, and benevolent is the Dharma of a Brahmin; to extend the four immeasurable minds with great compassion is the Dharma of a Brahmin; to attain the five supernormal powers is the Dharma of a Brahmin; and to transcend to the higher Brahma-heavens is the Dharma of a Brahmin."
"Now, having committed this violent assault, killing, and unrighteous violation of principle, I am filled with hesitation and remorse;
what should I do? He then went to the side of a crossroads beneath a tree, overwhelmed by grief, rage, and indignation.

Evil spirits aided the calamity, agitating and confusing his mind; with eyes wide with rage, he spat and glared about in all directions like a demonic lion, or like tigers, wolves, and beasts, leaping and bounding about with a terrifying appearance.

The four groups of practitioners were all heading toward the city; he then brandished his long sword and slaughtered many, so that none failed to flee in terror, with not a single one escaping, while those coming and going passed by without even noticing him.
Countless multitudes cried out in resentment and lamentation as they entered the royal palace, proclaiming:
"There is a rebellious traitor who has blocked the main thoroughfares and harmed many people; we pray only that the Heavenly King will eliminate this calamity for the sake of the people."
At that time, the bhikṣus entered the city for alms and saw those who had been informed of the situation in such a state of terror.
Having returned from their alms-round and finished their meal, they went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and addressed the World-Honored One:

"We have seen the people of the country gathered at the gate of the royal palace, announcing that there is a great rebel named Aṅgulimāla, who carries a sharp sword in his hand and causes harm to many; his hands and palms are stained with blood, and no one travels along the road."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Cease for a moment; I shall go to rescue them.
The Buddha rose from his seat and immediately proceeded to that place, where on the way he encountered herdsmen carrying loads upon their shoulders and riding on mounts.
The villagers addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"Great Sage, do not take this path; ahead lies a rebel who has blocked the four roads and slaughtered people in a bloody carnage. You must change your course, for you are traveling alone without any attendants."
The World-Honored One replied, "Even if the three realms were entirely overrun by bandits, I would not take them into account; how much less so a single thief?
Aṅgulimāla’s mother, wondering why her son had not returned, did not eat when mealtime arrived, fearing he must surely be starving.
He took provisions out of the city to provide for them there.

When midday was approaching and the hundred people were not yet complete, he feared that if the sun shifted past its zenith, his religious practice would remain incomplete; he thus intended to kill his mother to fulfill the required number.
The Buddha thought:
"If Aṅgulimāla harms his mother, his transgression will not cease and he cannot be saved.
The Buddha then suddenly stood before him. At that moment, seeing the Buddha leave his mother behind, Aṅgulimāla approached the World-Honored One with the stride of a lion, thinking to himself:

"When ten or a hundred men saw me charging forward, they did not dare to face me; I have always displayed my martial prowess with unrestrained freedom—how much more so against this śramaṇa who has come alone?"
"Now, my plan is to surely exterminate his life.

He then seized his sword and rushed toward the Buddha, yet he could not advance; though he exerted all his strength and ran with all his might, he still could not reach him. Thereupon, he thought to himself: "I have leaped across rivers and seas and unraveled all manner of bonds;
I have cast myself into battle with such valor that I have never had an equal opponent; no matter how heavy the gates or how firm the barriers, there were none I could not open or close."
"Yet this śramaṇa moves with such slow steps that I cannot catch up by running; though I exhaust all my power and might, I can never come near him.
Maṇḍūkapuṣpa said to the Buddha, "Śramaṇa, please stop!"
The Buddha said to the bandit,
"I have been staying here for many days, yet you alone have not stopped.
Then, Aṅgulimāla spoke from afar in verse:
"What does it mean for you, O Śramaṇa, to say that you have 'come to a standstill'?
To what does this statement refer, that you consider me to be 'not having come to a standstill'?
How can the Buddha now be established, while claiming that his bodily actions do not abide?"
"Since I am thus, I pray that you will explain and resolve this meaning.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke a verse for Aṅgulimāla, saying to him:
"Aṅgulimāla, listen to the Buddha’s abiding; the World-Honored One shall remove your transgressions."
"You run about with thoughts of ignorance; I shall certainly not stop you.
I abide securely in the three liberations, delighting in the Dharma and practicing the holy life;
you alone drive about with deluded thoughts, harboring malice that has not yet ceased."
"The Great Sage’s boundless wisdom praises tranquility at the crossroads;
having heard what he has said regarding transgression, I shall listen to and take up the chanting of the Dharma’s meaning.
Thereupon, Aṅgulimāla’s mind was immediately awakened; casting away his sword and prostrating himself, he threw himself upon the ground.
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will forgive my delusions and errors, and that you will look upon me with compassion as I seek the Way.

Relying on your compassionate transformation, I beg for forgiveness for my transgressions; may you deign to show mercy and provide succor, so that I may leave the household life and receive the precepts of accomplishment.”
The Buddha then conferred ordination upon him, and he immediately became a śramaṇa.

At that time, the World-Honored One, majestic and sublime in his majestic spiritual power, sat cross-legged amidst the radiance of wisdom, with the Venerable Aṅgulimāla attending him on his left and right, as they returned to the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Aṅgulimāla, having received this transformation and being trusted by the assembly, was likewise sustained by all the venerable disciples.

That son of noble family shaved off his beard and hair, donned the dharma-robes, and out of faith in the household life, left home for the path. He fulfilled the supreme, ultimate holy life (brahmacarya) and attained the six supernormal powers, realizing that birth and death were already severed.
Praising his pure virtues, [the Buddha] declared that he had accomplished what was to be done and understood the root of name-and-form, thereby attaining arhatship.

At that time, King Prasenajit (translated into Chinese as Heryue), accompanied by the fourfold army of elephants, horses, infantry, and cavalry, prepared his chariot for an expedition intending to punish the rebellious and impure. His body was exhausted and covered in dust as he passed by the Buddha’s dwelling and prostrated at his feet.
The Buddha asked the king,
"From where have you come, that your body is covered in dust?
The king addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Yes, World-Honored One!

There is a great rebel named Aṅgulimāla, fierce and violent, harboring malice and blocking the four highways. With a sharp blade in hand, he has injured and killed the people; we have now mobilized the fourfold assembly, intending to go forth and capture him."
At that time, Aṅgulimāla was present in the assembly, not far from the Buddha. The Buddha said to the king:
"Aṅgulimāla is here; having already shaved his hair and beard, he is now a bhikṣu. What do you think of him?"
The King addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Since he has already set his mind upon the Way, there is nothing that can be done; I shall provide him with food, clothing, bedding, seating, and medicine for his ailments for as long as I live.”
He asked the World-Honored One again:
"Indeed, Great Sage, how can a person who is cruel, harmful, and rebellious attain the Way and practice the meaning of tranquility?
Where does such a person now abide?"
The Buddha said to the king,
"Please sit here nearby.
When the king saw him from afar, fear immediately arose in his heart and the hair on his body stood on end.
The Buddha said, "Great King!
Do not be afraid; do not be anxious!"
"Now that you are benevolent and wise, there shall be no further opposition to my will.
The King performed a ritual greeting for him and said,
"O Wise One!..."
"Does this refer to a garland? He replied, "It does."
The king asked again,
"What is your clan name? He replied:
“Kikaṭa,” he asked again. “What is meant by ‘Kikaṭa’?”
He replied, “It is my father’s original surname.
The King said:
"Only the son of the Single-Horned One shall receive my offerings of clothing, food, bedding, and medicine for the sick throughout his entire life.
Having thus granted the request, the king prostrated himself in farewell and returned home. He praised the World-Honored One, saying:

"You are able to tame those who are untamed and bring to completion that which is unaccomplished. Abiding in peace, you bestow great compassion; there is nothing you do not open up through the Way. You subdue afflictions and rebellious forces, filling the assembly with the Dharma, and you cause even the common people to attain such discipline and concentration. My kingdom has many affairs, and I wish to take my leave."
The Buddha said,
"Go then, according to what you intend to practice.
The King prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and returned home.

At that time, the Venerable Aṅgulimāla was dwelling in seclusion, wearing the five-fold patched robe. Early the next morning, he took his alms bowl and entered the city of Śrāvastī to wander for alms. He saw women from various households who were pregnant; as their months were full and they faced the difficulty of childbirth, their hearts turned to him for refuge.
He asked Aṅgulimāla, “Where do you wish to go? Please grant me your protection.

Having received the offering, Aṅgulimāla left the city; when he had finished eating and washed his hands, he set aside the vessel and sat alone with deep reverence. He then approached the Buddha, prostrated himself, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"Early this morning, having donned my robes and taken up my alms bowl, I entered the city to beg for food. I saw a woman who was near her time to give birth; she was in distress due to difficult labor and, filled with fear, sought protection."
The Buddha told Aṅgulimāla:
"Go at once and say to the woman:

'If what Aṅgulimāla says is true and not false—if from birth until now you have never killed a living being—and if this is indeed so, sister, you shall immediately find peace and be free from affliction.'"
Aṅgulimāla said to the Buddha:
“I have committed countless crimes beyond measure; I have killed ninety-nine people, falling short of one hundred. Yet, to utter such a statement—is this not double-tongued speech?”
The World-Honored One said:

"In a previous life in another world, you were not the same person as in this present life; thus, your words were sincere and not false. It was by using such [truth] at that time that you rescued her from her distress."
Immediately following the holy command, he went to the woman’s side and spoke as the Buddha had instructed:
“If what I have spoken with utmost sincerity is not false—that since birth I have never taken life—and if this is indeed true, then may you, noble sister, be safe and sound in your delivery.”
Before he had finished speaking, the woman immediately gave birth, and the child was also safe and sound.

At that time, Aṅgulimāla entered the city of Śrāvastī; a group of young boys saw him and surrounded him, some throwing tiles and stones, some shooting arrows, some hacking and stabbing with knives, and others striking him with clubs.

The wise Aṅgulimāla, with his head wounded and his body injured, his clothes torn and tattered, returned to the place where the Buddha was. Prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, he stood before him and spoke in verse:
“I was formerly a bandit, My name, Aṅgulimāla, was renowned everywhere.
Now that the great abyss has been dried up, I take refuge in the Perfectly Awakened One.”
Thus he perfected patience; having reached the Buddha who transforms and enlightens the multitudes, he listened to the sūtras at the proper times, and for this reason he encountered no obstacles.
Now, having taken refuge in the Buddha and received the precepts of the True Dharma, [he remains steadfast].
Having attained the threefold penetration, one then accords with the teachings of all Buddhas.
Though in the past you harbored violent cruelty and took the lives of many living beings—
though in ancient times there was much peril— I am now known as the Harmless One.
Regarding transgressions committed by body or speech, or harboring a mind intent on killing—
so long as one does not endanger others, one shall never encounter calamities. Furthermore,
being free from past [karmic debts] and upholding the Dharma in tranquil stillness, one remains secure.
One who deserves the name "violent" becomes a benevolent sage through self-discipline.
By means of a single skillful means, one is tamed and settled, just as a hook tames wild elephants;
thus the Tathāgata has brought me to fulfillment, without sword and without staff.
If one was previously heedless but later becomes self-restrained,
that person will illuminate the world like the sun emerging from the clouds.
Even if one has committed many evils, as long as one does not sever one's manifold wholesome virtues, [one shall attain liberation].
That light illuminates the world, like the sun rising as the clouds disperse.
If a newly ordained bhikṣu diligently practices the Buddha’s teaching,
his light illuminates the world like the moon at its full.
Should one commit many offenses, one shall surely fall into the evil realms;
yet one need not fear further afflictions, for in consuming [the Dharma] there is no attachment.
One seeks not rebirth, nor has one ever encountered death through virtue.
One need only wait for the right time, keeping the mind constantly intent upon meditative concentration.
Thus, Aṅgulimāla, having already attained the state of an Arhat,
recited this verse before the World-Honored Buddha with his own mouth.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
The Venerable Aṅgulimāla and the assembly of bhikṣus, having heard this sutra, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
This is the *Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra* spoken by the Buddha.
